newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK's FTSE 100 nears 5,000 landmark.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK's FTSE 100 nears 5,000 landmark.

text.p: Britain's leading stock market index continued to defy the sceptics on Wednesday, surging towards the magical 5,000-point level despite the twin stumbling blocks of rising interest rates and strong sterling.

Just days after a poll of institutional investors revealed the most negative view towards British equities for a year, the blue chip FTSE index scored an all-time best of 4,991.8 points, bringing its year-to-date advance to 21.2 percent.
The FTSE ended 64.9 points higher at 4964.2.

Market players often say bull markets "climb a wall of worry," yet the market's sharp rise -- led by strong gains in heavyweight stocks such as Glaxo and HSBC Holdings -- has still shocked many market participants.

"One is slightly at a loss for words...It would not appear to be fundamentally justified but this is a very powerful move and one has to be careful about writing it off as madness," said Nick Knight, London-based strategist at Japanese broker Nomura.
The market's gains came despite last week's quarter point rate rise by the Bank of England, making Britain the only major western economy to be under the cosh of rising borrowing costs.
Those worries were shown on Monday in a poll by investment bank Merrill Lynch revealing British fund managers had swung to their most negative view on domestic stocks since last July.
Managers planning to cut their British share holdings were in an 18 percent majority, according to the poll of 56 institutions with 775 billion pounds of funds ($1.3 trillion).
Given that the market has been trading on multiples of earnings last seen before the crash of 1987, some pessimism could be justified.
Yet maybe institutions were saying one thing to Merrill's pollsters and doing another, because the FTSE's upward charge has continued unabated.
Pushed for an explanation, analysts said the FTSE 100 could appear better value than other leading equity markets, having underperformed for much of the early part of this year.
Equally interest rates could be near their peak and inflation may stay relatively subdued, providing a benign investment backdrop through 1998, they suggested.
Another theory is that overseas funds have been piling into leading British blue chips, helped by a touch of bid speculation in the banks and other sectors.
Yet some said the market's prime motor was more prosaic -- simply the high level of cash held by institutional investors.
Fund managers were sitting on a high level of cash when the market started to take off after the new Labour government's first budget on July 2.
Afraid of missing another leg to the two-and-a-half year old bull market, they started to move cash into shares, creating a shortage in big-cap companies and squeezing prices higher.
"There is certainly talk about 5,000 (on the FTSE 100)," one market-maker said. "There is still bid talk going on, there is cash around...this is a major squeeze."
Many participants have been left dazed and confused by the market's ebullience, given the negative effect of sterling's rise to 6-1/2 year highs against the mark.
Analysts have already downgraded estimates for companies such as Imperial Chemical Industries Plc and British Steel Plc because of the risk of weaker profits overseas.
They also point out the FTSE 250 index of mid-ranking stocks has missed out on the FTSE 100's rally and is about flat from its level at the start of 1997.
Either way, many participants have been hit by the stock market's unexpected strength and were increasingly reluctant to take a negative view.

"Sometime we will see a violent correction but the market could be 10 percent higher before that," one dealer said. "We have been bearish and we have been burnt and I don't want to get caught short again.".
